lesson.body:
Acidity is the tart, zingy quality in wine, the same brightness you taste in a squeeze of lemon or a green apple. Imagine sipping plain water, then biting into a lemon: the wine version of that wake-up is acidity. It is what makes a wine taste fresh and lively rather than dull. When a wine doesn't have enough acid to balance its body and weight, people call it "flabby" — soft and a bit lifeless, like flat soda.

You can actually feel acidity. Take a sip, swallow, and notice the sides of your tongue and the back of your cheeks. If your mouth starts watering and wants another sip, acidity is at work. Treat that watering as a yes/no signal that acidity is present, not a precise meter — how much you salivate varies by person and can be softened by sweetness, so an off-dry wine may taste gentler than its real acidity suggests.

Acidity is also why wine loves food, cutting through rich, fatty, or salty dishes like lemon on fish. White wines and cool-climate wines often feel especially crisp, since slow ripening preserves acid. Many reds are high in acid too; their tannin and body just mask it.
outcomes: Recognise acidity as wine's tart, mouth-watering freshness
Spot acidity by how your mouth waters
Explain why acidity makes wine good with food

deep_notes: The main acids in grapes are tartaric acid, which is fairly rare in other fruit, and malic acid, the sharp acid of green apples. Citric acid, the acid of lemons, is present only in small amounts. Tartaric acid is also behind the harmless crystals, nicknamed wine diamonds, that sometimes form on a cork or at the bottom of a bottle. They appear when wine gets cold and are not a fault.

Your mouth waters because acid triggers your salivary glands, which send saliva to dilute and neutralise it. That is why the effect carries on for a moment after you swallow. Many tasters feel acid first as a tingle along the sides of the tongue. Because sugar blunts the reaction, the same acid can feel sharp in a dry wine and gentle in a sweet one, so judge acidity and sweetness separately.

Acid does in wine what it does in cooking: it lifts and balances richness. Chefs finish rich sauces with lemon or vinegar for the same reason. A classic pairing is Champagne with fried food, where high acidity and bubbles leave your mouth feeling clean. Acidic food needs an acidic wine too: next to a tomato salad or a lemony dish, a low-acid wine can taste flat and dull.

In warm weather, grapes ripen fast and their acid, especially malic acid, drops as sugar rises. Cool regions such as the Mosel in Germany ripen grapes slowly, and Riesling is a naturally high-acid grape, so Mosel Rieslings taste racy, meaning lively and sharp. In hot places where acid falls too low, winemakers are often allowed to add tartaric acid. Among reds, Sangiovese, the grape of Chianti, and Barbera are known for high acid.

deeper.body: Great sweet wines need high acidity. Without it, the sugar feels heavy and sticky, a fault tasters call cloying. Tokaji from Hungary and sweet Rieslings from Germany are prized because their sharp acidity balances a lot of sugar, so each sip still feels fresh. In wine, balance matters more than the amount of any single thing.
deeper.title: Sweet wines need acid most

deeper.q: A sweet wine tastes sticky and heavy, with no freshness. What is it probably missing?
deeper.why: Acidity balances sugar. Without enough of it, a sweet wine turns cloying: heavy and sticky.

deeper.body: After the main fermentation, bacteria can turn sharp malic acid into lactic acid, the softer acid of yoghurt and soured milk. This is called malolactic conversion. Almost all red wines go through it. Many Chardonnays do too, which gives a rounder feel and sometimes a buttery note. Winemakers often block it in crisp whites like Riesling to keep their zing.
deeper.title: From apple to milk

deeper.q: Malolactic conversion makes a wine taste sharper and more acidic.
deeper.why: It does the opposite. Swapping sharp malic acid for gentler lactic acid makes the wine feel softer.

deeper.body: Winemakers track acidity partly with pH. The lower the number, the more acidic the liquid. Water sits at 7, while most wines fall between about 3 and 4, close to orange juice. The scale is logarithmic, meaning each whole step is a tenfold jump, so in chemical terms a wine at pH 3 is ten times as acidic as one at pH 4. It does not taste ten times as sharp, though.
deeper.title: Reading the pH number

deeper.q: Which of these is the most acidic?
deeper.why: On the pH scale, lower means more acidic, so the wine at 3.1 is the most acidic of these.

v2.body:
Ever found tiny glittering crystals under a cork? These **wine diamonds** are harmless crystals formed from **tartaric acid**, the most important acid in wine and fairly rare in other fruit. In 1848 the French scientist Louis Pasteur sorted crystals made from this wine acid with tweezers and found two mirror-image shapes, like a pair of gloves. It was the first clue that some molecules, the tiny parts everything is made of, come in left- and right-handed forms.

**Acidity** is the tart, zingy quality in wine, the same brightness you taste in a squeeze of lemon or a bite of green apple. It makes a wine taste fresh and lively rather than dull. A wine needs enough acid to balance its weight, meaning how heavy it feels in your mouth. Without it, the wine is **flabby**: soft and lifeless, like flat soda. With plenty, tasters call it crisp, and with a lot, racy, meaning lively and sharp.

You can feel acidity. Take a sip, swallow, and notice the sides of your tongue and the back of your cheeks. If your mouth starts to water, acidity is at work. Acid sets off your **salivary glands**, the parts of your mouth that make saliva (spit). The saliva waters the acid down, so the feeling lingers for a moment after you swallow.

Treat that watering as a yes or no signal, not a precise meter. How much you salivate varies from person to person, and **sweetness** softens it, so an off-dry (slightly sweet) wine may taste gentler than its real acidity suggests. So look for more than one clue:
• a watering mouth after you swallow
• a tingle along the sides of your tongue
• a tart, sharp taste, like citrus
• the context: a cool place, or a grape known for lots of acid

Acidity is also why wine loves food: it cuts through rich, fatty or salty dishes, like lemon on fish, and Champagne, the French sparkling wine, is a classic with fried food. Acidic food needs an acidic wine too: next to a tomato salad, a low-acid wine can taste flat.

As grapes ripen they lose acid and gain sugar. In **cool climates**, such as France's cooler north, grapes ripen slowly and keep their acid, so whites from Champagne or the Loire, or a Riesling from Germany's Mosel, taste crisp. Warm places in the south, such as Languedoc and the southern Rhône, make riper wines with less acid. Many reds are high in acid too, such as Sangiovese, the main grape of Italy's Chianti, and Barbera. In reds, **tannin** (the drying feel of strong tea) and a heavy, full feel can mask it.
deep_notes: The scientist was Louis Pasteur, and his crystals were salts of tartaric acid taken from winemaking. With a magnifying glass and tweezers he split them into right-handed and left-handed piles. Each pile, dissolved in water, twisted light in opposite directions. Winemakers knew the crust of these crystals in their barrels long before chemists did. Today many wineries chill wine close to freezing before bottling, called cold stabilisation, so the crystals form in the tank instead of on your cork.

The main acids in grapes are tartaric acid and malic acid, the sharp acid of green apples. Citric acid, the acid of lemons, is present only in small amounts. Tartaric acid matters most in wine because it keeps the wine chemically stable and helps hold its colour. So when a wine reminds you of lemon, it is the sensation you are recognising, not lemon's own acid.

Balance is the key idea. A light, delicate white can taste lovely with moderate acid, while a big, rich wine needs more to stay lively. Too much acid for the wine's weight can taste harsh or sour, too little tastes flabby. Professional tasters usually rate acidity as low, medium or high, and they judge it against the rest of the wine rather than on its own.

Many tasters feel acid twice: first as a slight prickle along the sides of the tongue while the wine is in the mouth, then as the mouth-watering after it has gone. Try it with a squeeze of lemon in a glass of water, then with plain water, and notice the difference. Practising with something familiar makes the feeling easier to spot in wine.

Saliva calms acid: it contains bicarbonate and phosphate, which make whatever is in your mouth less acidic. When a sharp wine arrives, your mouth answers with more saliva, and that flow is what you feel. Because people make different amounts of saliva, two friends can taste the same wine and disagree on how sharp it is. Neither is wrong; that is why one clue is never enough.

Sugar blunts the reaction to acid, so the same acid can feel sharp in a dry wine and gentle in a sweet one. That is why tasters judge acidity and sweetness separately. Context helps too: a Riesling from a cool region is a safe bet for high acid even if it is off-dry. Comparing two wines side by side is the easiest way to tell which has more.

Acid does in wine what it does in cooking: it lifts and balances richness. Chefs finish rich sauces with lemon or vinegar for the same reason. Champagne with fried food works because high acidity and bubbles leave your mouth feeling clean. The reverse matters too: with tomato, citrus dressings or goat's cheese, pick a wine with at least as much acid as the food.

In warm weather grapes ripen fast, and their acid, especially malic acid (the green-apple acid), drops as sugar rises. Cool regions such as the Mosel in Germany ripen grapes slowly, and Riesling is a naturally high-acid grape, so Mosel Rieslings taste racy. In hot places where acid falls too low, winemakers are often allowed to add tartaric acid, a step called acidification.

Sangiovese, the main grape of Chianti, and Barbera from Piedmont in northern Italy are known for high acid. That is why both are classic matches for tomato-based Italian food. In Sangiovese the firmer tannin grabs your attention first, so the acid is easy to miss. Barbera has soft tannin, so its acid shows more plainly, which makes it a good red to practise on. Ignore the drying feel for a moment and wait: if your mouth still waters after you swallow, the acid is there.

deeper.body: Great sweet wines need high acidity. Without it, the sugar feels heavy and sticky, a fault tasters call cloying. Tokaji from Hungary and sweet Rieslings from Germany are prized because their sharp acidity balances a lot of sugar, so each sip still feels fresh. In wine, balance matters more than the amount of any single thing.
deeper.title: Sweet wines need acid most

deeper.key: Acidity balances sugar; without enough of it, a sweet wine turns cloying.
deeper.q: A sweet wine tastes sticky and heavy, with no freshness. What is it probably missing?
deeper.remember: Sugar needs acid, or it cloys.
deeper.why: The best sweet wines, like Tokaji and sweet German Riesling, taste fresh because their acid is high.

deeper.body: After the main fermentation, when yeast turns sugar into alcohol, bacteria can turn sharp malic acid into lactic acid, the softer acid of yoghurt and soured milk. This is called malolactic fermentation. It is standard for almost all red wines and common for Chardonnay, giving a rounder feel and sometimes a buttery note. Winemakers often block it in crisp whites like Riesling to keep their zing.
deeper.title: From green apple to yoghurt

deeper.key: It swaps sharp malic acid for softer lactic acid, so the wine feels rounder.
deeper.q: Malolactic fermentation makes a wine taste sharper and more acidic.
deeper.remember: Malolactic: from apple sharp to yoghurt soft.
deeper.why: That is why winemakers often block it in crisp whites they want to keep zingy.

deeper.body: Winemakers track acidity partly with pH. The lower the number, the more acidic the liquid. Water sits at 7, while most wines fall between about 3 and 4, close to orange juice. The scale is logarithmic, meaning each whole step is a tenfold jump, so in chemical terms a wine at pH 3 is ten times as acidic as one at pH 4. It does not taste ten times as sharp, though.
deeper.title: Reading the pH number

deeper.key: On the pH scale, lower means more acidic, so pH 3.1 is the most acidic here.
deeper.q: Which of these is the most acidic?
deeper.why: pH helps winemakers judge freshness and stability, even though taste does not follow it exactly.
